triage.name: Bipolar Disorder
triage.reason: Major psychiatric illness with manic or depressive episodes; diagnosis by careful history of mood episodes, sleep and function, with strong safety and differential teaching.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Poor impulse control' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Focal neurologic deficit' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Bipolar I disorder affects men and women roughly equally; bipolar II disorder and rapid cycling are more common in women.

chief_complaints.text: My mood has been all over the place
I have times when I feel on top of the world and don't need sleep
Other times I feel really down and can't enjoy anything

hpi.onset: Usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood; the first episode may be depressive, manic, or mixed.
hpi.duration: Manic episodes last at least 7 days (or any duration if hospitalization is needed); depressive episodes last at least 14 days; hypomania lasts at least 4 days.
hpi.progression: Episodes develop over days to weeks and recur; some people have years of normal mood between episodes, while others have frequent cycling.
hpi.quality: Manic moods are elevated, expansive, or irritable; depressive moods are sad, empty, or hopeless.
hpi.severity: May be mild (hypomania) to severe with psychosis or high suicide risk.
hpi.timing: Episodes can happen at any time, but sleep disruption often precedes mania.

associated_symptoms.text: Talking faster and louder than usual
Needing little or no sleep but still full of energy
Acting impulsively, such as spending sprees, reckless sex, or foolish business decisions
Feeling sad or empty most of the day
Losing interest or pleasure in almost all activities
Sleeping too much or too little
Sleeping too much during depressive episodes

pertinent_negatives: Symptoms only during a medical illness
Mood changes lasting less than 4 days
Psychotic symptoms persisting between mood episodes

positives.text: Loss of interest in usual activities

argues_against: Psychotic symptoms continuously for 2 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms

positives.text: Decreased need for sleep during high periods

atypical.how_it_differs: Irritability and rapid mood shifts are more prominent than discrete euphoric episodes; symptoms often overlap with ADHD.
More depressive and mixed presentations, less euphoric mania, more cognitive complaints and medical comorbidity.
Risk of relapse is high, especially postpartum; mood episodes can be severe and include psychosis.

general.mild: Alert, animated, talkative; may be distractible but cooperative.
general.moderate: Pressured speech, increased motor activity, may be irritable or euphoric; no psychosis.
general.severe: Markedly agitated, loud, possibly threatening or disorganized; psychosis may be present.
general.critical: Extreme agitation or catatonia; severe impulsivity with high risk of harm to self or others.

findings.maneuver: Observe mood and affect during interview
Ask about mood and observe reactions
Listen to rate and rhythm of speech
findings.finding: Rapid, loud, and difficult to interrupt speech
Thoughts jump rapidly from topic to topic
Inflated self-esteem or unrealistic beliefs about abilities

findings.maneuver: Notice whether the patient attends to irrelevant stimuli
findings.finding: Easily drawn away by unimportant details

findings.maneuver: Ask about mood and observe affect
Ask directly about thoughts of death or suicide
findings.finding: Expresses wish to be dead or plans for suicide
No focal weakness, sensory loss, or asymmetry

findings.maneuver: Ask patient to hold arms outstretched with fingers spread

initial.why: Baseline blood count before medication; rule out anemia or infection contributing to mood symptoms
Electrolytes and renal function before lithium or other mood stabilizers
Rule out thyroid dysfunction that can mimic mania or depression
Identify substances that can cause or worsen mood episodes

initial.only_if: any patient who could be pregnant

initial.why: Screen for lifetime manic or hypomanic symptoms

confirmatory.why: Standardized diagnostic interview to confirm mood episodes and rule out other psychiatric disorders

supporting.why: Assess severity of current depressive symptoms
Assess severity of current manic symptoms

not_indicated.only_if: focal neurologic deficits or atypical presentation suggesting a structural brain lesion
suspected seizure disorder or rapid cycling with confusion

decision_points: Pregnancy test before starting mood stabilizers
Check TSH and urine toxicology to rule out secondary causes of mood symptoms
Assess suicide risk and need for hospitalization

criteria.name: DSM-5 Bipolar I disorder (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: At least one manic episode lasting at least 7 days or requiring hospitalization; may be preceded or followed by hypomanic or major depressive episodes.

criteria.name: DSM-5 Bipolar II disorder (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: At least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode; no full manic episode.

criteria.name: DSM-5 Cyclothymic disorder (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Numerous periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms lasting at least 2 years (1 year in children and adolescents) without meeting full criteria for hypomanic or major depressive episodes.

differential.name: Substance/medication-induced mood disorder
differential.why_considered: Mania or depression appearing during substance intoxication, withdrawal, or after starting a medication that can affect mood.
differential.trigger: Recent stimulant use, corticosteroid prescription, or other substance exposure

history: Symptoms begin within days to weeks of starting a medication or substance
Heavy or recent use of stimulants, cocaine, alcohol, or corticosteroids
Symptoms improve after the substance is stopped
No prior mood episodes before substance use
exam: Dilated pupils, tremor, tachycardia, or other signs of intoxication
No chronic pattern of mood episodes between substance exposures

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Manic-like symptoms of irritability, insomnia, weight loss, and increased energy.
differential.trigger: Unexplained weight loss, heat intolerance, goiter, or tremor

history: Weight loss despite increased appetite
Heat intolerance
Diarrhea
Palpitations
Anxiety rather than true euphoria or grandiosity
imaging: Increased radioactive iodine uptake in Graves disease

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Depressive symptoms identical to the depressive episodes of bipolar disorder.

history: No history of hypomanic or manic episodes
Symptoms are consistently depressive without periods of elevated or irritable mood
May have first episode at any age
Family history of unipolar depression rather than bipolar disorder
exam: Depressed affect, psychomotor retardation or agitation
No evidence of current mania or hypomania

differential.name: Borderline personality disorder
differential.why_considered: Mood swings, irritability, impulsivity, and self-harm can resemble bipolar disorder.

history: Mood shifts happen within hours and are usually triggered by interpersonal events
Chronic feelings of emptiness
Fear of abandonment
Recurrent self-harm and suicidal gestures
Identity disturbance
No sustained periods of decreased need for sleep or grandiosity
exam: Affect is reactive to discussion of relationships

differential.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
differential.why_considered: Hyperactivity, distractibility, and impulsivity can be mistaken for mania, especially in children and adolescents.

history: Symptoms began before age 12
Chronic, pervasive inattention and hyperactivity rather than episodic mood changes
No distinct periods of elevated or irritable mood with decreased need for sleep
Problems in school and work due to attention rather than mood

differential.name: Schizoaffective disorder
differential.why_considered: Psychotic symptoms and mood episodes overlap, making the distinction subtle.

history: Psychotic symptoms occur for at least 2 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms
Chronic course of psychosis
Negative symptoms such as flat affect or social withdrawal
No clear return to baseline between mood episodes

severity.mild: Hypomanic symptoms or mild depression; mood changes are noticeable but do not cause major functional impairment, no psychosis, no suicidal ideation.
severity.moderate: Full manic or major depressive episode with clear impairment; pressured speech, agitation or psychomotor retardation, distractibility, but no psychosis; may have passive thoughts of death without a plan.
severity.severe: Severe mania or depression with psychosis, severe agitation, marked functional impairment, or active suicidal ideation with a plan; may require hospitalization.
severity.critical: Life-threatening: catatonia, severe agitation with risk of harm to self or others, suicidal behavior with high lethality, or medical complications such as dehydration and exhaustion from a prolonged severe episode.

red_flags.finding: Active suicidal ideation with plan or intent
red_flags.meaning: High risk for suicide; requires emergency psychiatric evaluation and hospitalization.

red_flags.finding: Catatonia, such as stupor, mutism, posturing, or negativism
red_flags.meaning: Can progress to medical complications; may require benzodiazepines or electroconvulsive therapy.

red_flags.finding: Psychotic features such as command hallucinations or paranoid delusions
red_flags.meaning: Severe episode with increased risk of harm; may indicate schizoaffective disorder if psychosis persists outside mood episodes.
Danger to self or others; may need emergency sedation and safety measures.

red_flags.finding: Dehydration, weight loss, or diminished oral intake
red_flags.meaning: Medical compromise from severe mania or depression; needs stabilization.

red_flags.finding: Mixed features with simultaneous manic and depressive symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Higher suicide risk and worse prognosis.

red_flags.finding: New or worsening agitation after starting an antidepressant
red_flags.meaning: May be antidepressant-induced mania; stop or adjust the antidepressant and evaluate for bipolar disorder.

complications.name: Substance use disorder
clues: Use of alcohol or drugs to manage mood

special_populations.differences: More irritability and rapid mood shifts than classic euphoric mania; symptoms overlap with ADHD; diagnosis often delayed.
More depressive and mixed presentations, less euphoria; cognitive complaints and medical comorbidity complicate diagnosis; lower medication doses often needed.
High risk of relapse, especially postpartum; many mood stabilizers are teratogenic; requires specialized perinatal psychiatric care.
Lithium is contraindicated or requires careful monitoring; renal function must be checked before and during treatment.
Antipsychotics and some mood stabilizers can worsen weight and glucose; choose medications with lower metabolic risk.

key_questions.question: Have you had periods of several days or longer when you felt unusually high, euphoric, or irritable and had more energy than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Manic or hypomanic episode: elevated, expansive, or irritable mood for at least 7 days (mania) or 4 days (hypomania).

key_questions.question: During those periods, did you need less sleep than usual but still feel rested and full of energy?
key_questions.looking_for: Decreased need for sleep, a hallmark of mania.

key_questions.question: Have you had periods lasting at least two weeks when you felt sad, empty, or hopeless or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?
What was the timing and duration of these mood episodes? Did anything seem to bring them on?
key_questions.looking_for: Episodes lasting days to weeks; triggers such as sleep deprivation, stress, or substance use.

key_questions.question: During the high periods, did you do things that were risky or out of character, like spending sprees, reckless driving, or impulsive sexual behavior?
key_questions.looking_for: Impulsivity, poor judgment, and risk-taking during elevated mood.

key_questions.question: Have you had thoughts of death or suicide? Have you made a plan or attempted suicide in the past?
key_questions.looking_for: Suicidal ideation, plan, intent, or prior attempts; current safety risk.

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with a mental health condition or been hospitalized for a psychiatric problem?
key_questions.looking_for: History of mood episodes, hospitalizations, or prior psychiatric treatment.

key_questions.question: What medications have you tried, including antidepressants? Did any of them make your mood go too high or cause you to feel unusually energized?
key_questions.looking_for: Antidepressant-induced mania or hypomania, which suggests bipolar disorder.

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have bipolar disorder, depression, or have they attempted suicide?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of bipolar disorder or mood disorders, increasing risk.

key_questions.question: Do you use any substances, alcohol, or stimulants? Have you used any recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Substance use can trigger or mimic mood episodes; need to rule out substance-induced mood disorder.

key_questions.question: Have you had symptoms like weight loss, heat intolerance, tremors, or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Hyperthyroidism can mimic mania; screen for thyroid dysfunction.

key_questions.question: Are you hearing voices or seeing things others don't, or having beliefs that others find unusual?
key_questions.looking_for: Psychotic features indicating severe episode and increased risk; may need urgent intervention.

reasoning_points: Presence of at least one manic or hypomanic episode characterized by elevated, expansive, or irritable mood, increased energy, and associated symptoms such as decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, or risky behavior.
Depressive episodes are common but not required if mania is clearly present (for bipolar I); bipolar II requires both hypomanic and depressive episodes, with no full manic episode.
Symptoms are not due to substance use, a medication, or another medical condition such as hyperthyroidism (supported by normal thyroid function and negative toxicology).
Family history of bipolar disorder, early age of onset, and prior antidepressant-induced mania increase the likelihood of the diagnosis.
Safety assessment shows current suicidal ideation or psychosis, requiring appropriate level of care and urgent management.

easy: Classic young adult with clear manic episode: euphoric mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, and no substance use or medical cause.
Family history of bipolar disorder and prior episodes consistent with mania and depression.
medium: Patient presents with a depressive episode and does not spontaneously report past hypomanic episodes; screening questions reveal a prior 4-day period of elevated mood and decreased need for sleep.
Mixed features: simultaneous depressive and manic symptoms, increasing suicide risk and diagnostic complexity.
Comorbid substance use that could also cause mood symptoms, requiring careful timeline to establish primary bipolar disorder.
hard: Rapid cycling (4 or more mood episodes per year) with blurred episode boundaries and poor insight; no collateral information available.
Psychotic features such as paranoid delusions or command hallucinations, making it hard to distinguish from schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia.
Late-life onset of mania with cognitive complaints and medical comorbidities; must rule out neurological causes and medication effects.
Pregnant patient with bipolar disorder, needing careful medication management and high risk of relapse, especially postpartum.
